newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila rate cuts seen to briefly weaken peso.
newsitem.headline: Manila rate cuts seen to briefly weaken peso.

text.p: The Philippine Central Bank's cut in overnight rates on Wednesday signals the bank is comfortable with the pace of economic growth, but the move should slightly weaken the peso, analysts and traders said.
The Central Bank rate cuts come on the heels of a 0.25 percentage point increase in U.S. interest rates on Tuesday.

Due to the Central Bank's action, the bellwether 91-day Treasury bill rate could go down to as low as 9.0 percent in the next few months and the peso is expected to trade in a lower range of 26.35/26.45 from the previous 26.30/26.35, analysts said.
Last Monday, the 91-day T-bill rate stood at 9.724 percent.
On Wednesday, the Central Bank trimmed its overnight borrowing rate to 9.9 percent from 10.0 percent and its overnight lending rate to 12.65 percent from 12.75 percent.
Central Bank Governor Gabriel Singson told Reuters earlier in an interview that the rate cuts were in line with the trend in domestic interest rates.
He also said the Central Bank is comfortable with the level of the peso as long as there is no speculation in the currency.
Joey Cuyegkeng, research head of ING Barings Securities, said, "We're in a situation of adjustment towards a new equilibrium between interest rates and the peso-dollar rate."

"Fundamentals show interest rates should go down. Between now and the next reserve requirement cut in July, we expect no turbulence from the inflation side...We see a further flattening of the yield curve," Antonio Agcaoili, treasurer of Banco Santander in Manila, said on Wednesday.
"We likewise see a stable foreign exchange rate. The Central Bank has instilled a lot of confidence in the market," Agcaoili added.
The Central Bank's willingness to nudge rates down further suggests that it is at ease with the economy's low inflation, analysts said.
Inflation at the retail level was 4.4 percent in February, down from five percent in January.

"It (the Central Bank's move) just shows the good fundamentals of the Philippine economy. We're still confident of further growth with low inflation," said Paul Joseph Garcia, an economist at Metrobank.

Though the peso had fallen to 26.37 on Wednesday due to the higher U.S. interest rate and lower domestic rates, such weakness is expected to be brief as the currency was quick to recover when similar Philippine rate cuts occurred in the past few weeks, Santander's Agcaoili said.
Bank traders said the peso is currently reeling from the departure of arbitrage money due to the lower interest premium of the peso over the U.S. dollar which they estimate at 1.904 percentage point.

"The Central Bank has been successful in keeping rates steady," Agcaoili said, noting that the Central Bank is armed with a high level of gross international reserves. "We likewise see a continuous inflow of direct foreign investments," he said.
